# If Edge Coloring is Hard under SETH, then SETH is False Alexander S. Kulikov ∗
Ivan Mihajlin † **Abstract** The Edge Coloring problem is notoriously hard: it is still unknown whether it can be solved in time 2_o(n_2) (let alone 2_O(n_)), where _n_ is the number of nodes of the input graph. Can one explain the lack of such upper bounds by deriving a lower bound \(2^{\Omega(n^2)}\) from a lower bound for SAT, 3-SUM, or APSP? In this note, we provide a negative answer for this question: if there is a reduction showing that Edge Coloring cannot be solved faster than in \(\alpha^{n^2}\) (where \(\alpha>1\) is an explicit constant) under a hypothesis that known algorithms for one of the problems mentioned above are optimal, then the corresponding hypothesis is false. ## 1 Overview of New Results The field of fine-grained complexity aims to establish tight connections between complexity of computational problems. A fine-grained reduction, denoted \((P,p(n))\le(Q,q(n))\), implies that a faster than _q(n_)-time algorithm for _Q_ leads to a faster than _p(n_)-time algorithm for _P_. Equivalently, it says that if _P_ cannot be solved faster than in _p(n_) time, then _Q_ cannot be solved faster than in _q(n_) time. The standard assumptions in this field are hardness of Satisfiability (SAT) [13, 14], 3-SUM [10, 9], Orthogonal Vectors (OV) [18], All Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) [19], Online Matrix- Vector Multiplication [12], and Set Cover [8]. For example, assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (stating that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists _k_ such that _k_-SAT cannot be solved in time \(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}\)), the following upper bounds are essentially optimal: 2_n_ for Hitting Set (where _n_ is the size of the universe), 2_n_ for NAE-SAT (where _n_ is the number of the variables) [8], _nk_ for _k_-Dominating Set [17] (where _n_ is the number of nodes in the input graph and \(k\ge 7\)), 2tw for Independent Set [16] (where tw is the treewidth of the input graph). In the Edge Coloring problem (also known as Chromatic Index), one is given an undirected graph and is asked to color the edges using the minimum number of colors such that any two edges sharing a node receive different colors. The best known algorithm for Edge Coloring transforms an input graph with _n_ nodes and _m_ edges into a line graph with _m_ nodes and finds its chromatic index in time _O_∗(2_m_) [5]. (The \(O^*(\cdot)\) notation suppresses polynomial factors.) As _m_ can be as large as \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}\), the running time can be as bad as \(2^{\Omega(n^2)}\). It is not known whether Edge Coloring can be solved in time 2_o(n_2). It is natural to ask whether one can prove a lower bound \(2^{\Omega(n^2)}\) for Edge Coloring under an assumption that SAT, 3-SUM, or APSP is hard. We give a negative answer to this question. **Theorem 1.** _If there exists a fine-grained reduction showing that, assuming SETH, Edge Coloring cannot be solved in time_ \(\alpha^{n^2}\)_, for some_ \(\alpha>1\)_, then SETH is false._ ∗JetBrains Research. Email: `alexander.s.kulikov@gmail.com`. †JetBrains Research. Email: `ivmihajlin@gmail.com`.

The theorem above connects two specific problems, Edge Coloring and SAT. We generalize the theorem by showing that instead of Edge Coloring one can use any problem whose conjectured upper bound is truly exponential with respect to the bit-length of the input, and instead of SAT one can use any efficiently self-reducible problem. Namely, denote by _s_ the bit-length of an input. (We assume that a bit encoding of a problem is fixed. For all problems considered later in the text, we will specify an encoding.) Informally, we say that a problem is efficiently self-reducible if one can reduce an instance of the problem to a number of sufficiently smaller instances of the same problem. The formal definition is given later in the text (see Definition 2). It is known that SAT, APSP, and 3-SUM are efficiently self-reducible. Using the two just introduced notions, the generalization of Theorem 1 states that fine-grained reductions cannot establish truly exponential complexity lower bounds: if there exists a fine-grained reduction showing that, assuming that _P_ cannot be solved faster than in _p(s_), _Q_ cannot be solved faster than in \(\beta^s\), then _P_ can be solved in time \(p(s)^{1-\varepsilon}\).

**Theorem 2.** _Let P be an efficiently self-reducible problem,_ \(p:\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) _be a non-decreasing and efficiently computable function, and Q be a problem that can be solved in time_ \(O(\beta^s)\)_, where_ \(\beta>1\) _is a constant. Then, if there exists a fine-grained reduction_ \((P,p(s))\le(Q,\gamma^s)\)_, for a constant_ \(\gamma>1\)_, then P can be solved in time_ \(p(s)^{1-\epsilon}\) _for some constant_ \(\epsilon>0\).

An immediate corollary of this theorem is that there are no efficiently self-reducible problems of truly exponential complexity: if _P_ can be solved in time \(\alpha^s\) and a fine-grained reduction proves that _P_ cannot be solved faster than in \(\beta^s\), then this reduction can be used to solve _P_ in time \(\gamma^s\), where \(\gamma<\beta\).

## 1.1 Known Barriers to Hardness Proofs

Our result is close in spirit to \[1, Theorem 3.1\] where it is shown that if the Longest Common Subsequence is \(O(n^2/\mathrm{log}^\alpha n)\)-hard (for some constant \(\alpha>0\)) under SETH, then SETH is false. There are also two general "hardness of proving hardness" results that show that proving hardness under SETH is difficult as it implies circuit lower bounds. Namely, in \[7\], it is shown that if APSP or 3-SUM is hard under SETH, then NSETH (nondeterministic version of SETH) is false implying new circuit lower bounds. In \[4\], it is shown that lower bounds of the form \(\alpha^n\) under SETH for various problems including Hamiltonian Path, Graph Coloring, Independent Set, _k_-Path, _k_-Set Splitting (and many others including parameterized problems) would lead to new Boolean or arithmetic circuit lower bounds.

## 1.2 Upwards Reductions

Speaking about problems parameterized by bit-length _s_, Theorem 2 says that fine-grained reductions cannot go too high, that is, they are unable to prove a lower bound of the form \(\alpha^s\). It is interesting to note that fine-grained reductions from the literature, viewed as reductions between problems parameterized by _s_, almost never go upwards, see Figure 1. Intuitively, this is because, usually, a fine-grained reduction does not shrink its input length. At the same time, this intuition cannot be made formal as there exist synthetic upwards reductions: take a language \(P\in\mathsf{DTIME}[s^3]\) and define a language \(P'\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) as follows: for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^*\), \(x\in P\) if and only if \(x01^{|x|^2}\in P'\). Then, clearly, \((P',O(s^{1.5}))\le(P,O(s^3))\).

## 2 General Setting

### 2.1 Fine-grained Reductions

**Definition 1.** _Let P,Q be problems,_ \(p,q:\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) _be non-decreasing functions, and_ \(\delta:\mathbb{R}_{>0}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{>0}\)_. We say that_ \((P,p(n))\delta\)-fine-grained reduces _to_ (_Q,q(n_)) _and write_ \((P,p(n))\le_\delta\left(Q,q(n)\right)\)_, if for every_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _and_ \(\delta=\delta(\varepsilon)>0\)_, there exists an algorithm_ A _for P with oracle access to Q, a constant_ \(\alpha\)_, and a function_ \(t(n):\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\)_, such that on any instance of P of size n, the algorithm_ A

• _runs in time at most_ \(\alpha\cdot(p(n))^{1-\delta}\);<tbc>

• _produces at most t(n_) _instances of Q adaptively: every instance depends on the previously produced instances as well as their answers of the oracle for Q;_<tbc>

• _the sizes n<sub>i</sub> of the produced instances satisfy the inequality_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\sum_{i=1}^{t(n)}q(n_i)^{1-\varepsilon}\le\alpha\cdot(p(n))^{1-\delta}.\)<tbc>

Figure 1: A partial web of known fine-grained reductions. We assume the following encoding of the input for various problems. For problems dealing with sequences of _n_ integers (Orthogonal Vectors, _k_-SUM, Edit Distance), the input is encoded in binary directly. Since one can assume that that the integers have absolute values bounded by a polynomial in _n_, \(s=\Theta(nlogn)\). For problems dealing with sparse graphs (Sparse All Pairs Max Flows and Sparse Diameter), the input is given as a list of edges, hence \(s=\Theta(nlogn)\). For the remaining graph problems, the input graph can be dense, so we encode it as its adjacency matrix, hence \(s=\Theta(n^2)\). For _k_-SAT, the input is a list of _m_ clauses, each of length at most _k_, hence \(s=\Theta(mlogn)\).

We say that (_P,p(n_)) _fine-grained reduces_ to (_Q,q(n_)) and write \((P,p(n))\le(Q,q(n))\) if \((P,p(n))\le_\delta(Q,q(n))\) for some function \(\delta:\mathbb{R}_{>0}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{>0}\).

If \((P,p(n))\le(Q,q(n))\), then any improvement over the running time _q(n_) for the problem _Q_ implies an improvement over the running time _p(n_) for the problem _P_: for any \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(\delta>0\), such that if _Q_ can be solved in time \(O(q(n)^{1-\varepsilon})\), then _P_ can be solved in time \(O(p(n)^{1-\delta})\).

### 2.2 Standard Hardness Hypotheses

The most frequently used hardness assumptions in fine-grained reductions are the following.

**SETH:** for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists _k_ such that _k_-SAT cannot be solved in time \(O(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n})\).

**3-SUM Hypothesis:** for every \(\varepsilon>0\), 3-SUM cannot be solved in time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\).

**APSP Hypothesis:** for every \(\varepsilon>0\), APSP cannot be solved in time \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\).

### 2.3 Efficient Self-reducibility

Here, we formalize the notion of efficient self-reducibility as a fine-grained reduction from a problem to smaller instances of the same problem. This notion may be viewed as a fine-grained version of the notion of strong downward self-reducibility introduced in \[11\].

**Definition 2.** _Let P be a problem and_ \(p:\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) _be a non-decreasing function. We say that P is_ efficiently self-reducible for _p(n), if for any_ \(0<\alpha<1\) _there exists a fine-grained reduction_ \((P,p(n))\le(P,p(n))\) _such that the size_ \(n'\) _of every instance solved by an oracle satisfies_

\(p(n')\le p(n)^\alpha.\) (1)

In a sense, efficient self-reducibility says that to solve _P_ faster than in _p(n_) time, it suffices to design a faster than _p(n_) time algorithm for small size instances.

It is known that problems from popular hardness assumptions satisfy this property.

• SAT is efficiently self-reducible for 2_<sup>n</sup>_: branch on all but \(\alpha n\) variables to get \(2^{n(1-\alpha)}\) instances each depending on \(\alpha n\) variables (inequality (1) turns into \(2^{\alpha n}\le(2^n)^\alpha\)).<tbc>

• APSP is efficiently self-reducible for _n_<sup>3</sup> as APSP is equivalent to min-plus matrix multiplication: to multiply two \(n\times n\)-matrices, break them into \(n^\alpha\times n^\alpha\)-matrices; then, it remains to multiply \(n^{3-3\alpha}\) matrices of size \(n^\alpha\times n^\alpha\) (inequality (1) turns into \((n^\alpha)^3\le(n^3)^\alpha\)).<tbc>

• 3-SUM is efficiently self-reducible for _n_<sup>2</sup>: an instance of size _n_ can be reduced to \(O(n^{2-2\alpha})\) instances of size \(n^\alpha\) as shown in \[15\] (inequality (1) turns into \((n^\alpha)^2\le(n^2)^\alpha\)).

## 3 Impossibility of Reductions to Exponentially Hard Problems

In this section, we prove the main result: if Edge Coloring is \(\alpha^{n^2}\)-hard under SETH, then SETH is false. We then generalize this result by replacing Edge Coloring with any problem whose conjectured bound is truly exponential in terms of the input bit-length and SAT with any self-reducible problem. The main idea of the proof is the following. Using a reduction from SAT to Edge Coloring, we design an algorithm that solves SAT faster than in 2_<sup>n</sup>_. To this end, similarly to the Method<tbc>

of Four Russians, we start by preparing a look-up table containing answers for all Edge Coloring instances of certain small size \(n'\). Because of the truly exponential time complexity of Edge Coloring, the running time of this step is only polynomially slower than solving a single Edge Coloring instance of size \(n'\). Then, using efficient self-reducibility of SAT, we reduce a given CNF formula to a bunch of sufficiently small formulas. Finally, using the assumed fine-grained reduction and the prepared look-up table, we solve SAT for each of the resulting formulas faster than the brute force search.

**Theorem 1.** _If there exists a fine-grained reduction showing that, assuming SETH, Edge Coloring cannot be solved in time_ \(\alpha^{n^2}\)_, for some_ \(\alpha>1\)_, then SETH is false._

_Proof._ Assume that there exists a reduction<tbc>

\((\mathsf{SAT},2^n)\le(\mathsf{Edge Coloring},\alpha^{n^2}).\)

<tbc>This is an algorithm A that checks whether an input formula with _n_ variables is satisfiable by making oracle calls to an algorithm for Edge Coloring. The main property of A is that it solves SAT in time \(2^{(1-\delta)n}\), for a \(\delta>0\), if the oracle solves Edge Coloring in time \(\alpha^{n^2/2}\) for some \(\delta>0\). This implies that if A makes an oracle call to a graph with _t_ nodes, then \(\alpha^{t^2/2}\le 2^{(1-\delta)n}\), hence

\(t\le\left(\frac{2(1-\delta)n}{log_2\alpha}\right)^\frac{1}{2}.\) (2)

Using this observation, we can design a faster than 2_<sup>n</sup>_ algorithm for SAT by designing an efficient oracle for Edge Coloring. To do this, we solve Edge Coloring for every graph with at most _k_=(_n/_2)<sup>1/2</sup> nodes and save the result in a table. Each graph on at most _k_ nodes can be specified by a characteristic 0/1-vector of \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{2}\) potential edges. Solving Edge Coloring on such a graph takes time \(O^*(2^\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{2})\) \[5\]. Hence, the total running time of this stage is<tbc>

\(O^*(2^\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{2})=O^*(2^{k^2})=O^*(2^{n/2}).\)

<tbc>To check satisfiability of a given formula _F_ with _n_ variables, branch on all but \(\beta n\) variables, for a parameter \(\beta\) to be chosen later. It suffices to solve SAT for the resulting \(2^{(1-\beta)n}\) formulas. Due to (2), on every such formula, A calls the oracle for Edge Coloring on graphs with at most

\(\left(\frac{2(1-\delta)\beta n}{log_2\alpha}\right)^{1/2}\)

nodes. By choosing \(\beta=\frac{log_2\alpha}{4(1-\delta)}>0\), we ensure that the answers for all such graphs are already in the table (computed at the preprocessing stage). This way, we can answer all oracle calls quickly meaning that A solves SAT for every formula with \(\beta n\) variables in time \(2^{(1-\delta)\beta n}\).

The resulting algorithm for checking satisfiability of a formula with _n_ variables prepares an oracle, branches on all but \(\beta n\) variables, and solves SAT of the resulting \(2^{(1-\beta)n}\) formulas using the algorithm A with the constructed oracle. Its running time is

\(O^*\left(max\left\{2^{n/2},2^{(1-\beta)n}\cdot 2^{(1-\delta)\beta n}\right\}\right)=O^*\left(2^{(1-\sigma)n}\right),\)

where \(\sigma=min\{1/2,\delta\beta\}>0\).

**Theorem 2.** _Let P be an efficiently self-reducible problem,_ \(p:\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) _be a non-decreasing and efficiently computable function, and Q be a problem that can be solved in time_ \(O(\beta^s)\)_, where_ \(\beta>1\) _is a constant. Then, if there exists a fine-grained reduction_ \((P,p(s))\le(Q,\gamma^s)\)_, for a constant_ \(\gamma>1\)_, then P can be solved in time_ \(p(s)^{1-\epsilon}\) _for some constant_ \(\epsilon>0\).

_Proof._ If we apply the reduction from an instance of the problem _P_ of size _a_, then all of the oracle calls made by reductions would be on instances of the problem _Q_ of size at most \(b=\frac{logp(a)}{log\gamma}\) . With this in mind, we are going to enumerate and solve all of the instances of the problem _Q_ of size up to \(\nu\), for some \(\nu\) to be determined later. This will take time \(O(2^\nu\beta^\nu=O((2\beta)^\nu)\). Then, we use self-reducibility of _P_ to reduce an instance of size _s_ to some number of instances of size at most \(p^{-1}(p(s)^\alpha)\) for some \(0<\alpha<1\) to be determined later. We apply the given reduction from _P_ to _Q_ to each of the new small instances. Whenever the reduction makes an oracle call, we can just take a peek into the lookup table. To do this, we will need to have

\(\nu\ge\frac{logp(p^{-1}(p(s)^\alpha))}{log\gamma}=\frac{logp(s)^\alpha}{log\gamma}=\frac{\alpha}{log\gamma}logp(s).\) (3)

On the other hand, we need<tbc>

\(O((2\beta)^\nu)\le p(s)^\frac{1}{2}.\)

<tbc>This gives us

\(\nu\le\frac{1}{2log2\beta}logp(s).\)

We can pick \(\nu=\frac{1}{2log2\beta}logp(s)\) and then choose \(\alpha>0\) to make the inequality (3) correct too.

Overall, we have a preprocessing that takes time _p(s_)<sup>1/2</sup> and a fine-grained reduction that solves all of the oracle calls in polynomial time. By the properties of fine-grained reduction this means that we will solve all the small instances of _P_ in time

\(O(p(s)^{1/2}+p(s)^{(1-\delta)})=O(p(s)^{1-\delta})\)

for some \(\delta>0\).
